data.title: The Clarity Act is DEAD
data.transcript_raw: The most heavily lobbied piece of legislation in crypto's history just went to the Senate floor and lost 49 to 50. But, the weird thing is the Senate didn't reject the Clarity Act. It actually refused to debate it at all because that vote wasn't about passing anything. It was a cloture vote on the motion to proceed, which is political language for are we allowed to start talking about this? So, 2 years of lobbying work and a crypto war chest that started the cycle at $193 million and the industry still couldn't buy permission to open the conversation. So, what actually killed [music] Clarity and what happens now? Well, to answer those questions, we'll look at why a technical market structure bill became a political issue, why the timing makes this final, and who ends up writing crypto's rulebook now that Congress has walked away from it. My name is Guy and this [music] is the Coin Bureau. So, what was actually on the table here? Well, Clarity was supposed to be the ultimate crypto rulebook. It drew a line between two agencies, the CFTC, which would take primary oversight of decentralized coins like Bitcoin, and the SEC, which would keep the ones still behaving like securities. It set a definitive test for when a token stops being a security, structured around whether insiders still have control over supply and governance. It gave exchanges a federal registration path and customer fund segregation rules written specifically so nobody could commingle client money the way FTX did. And it carved out protections for developers, node operators, and validators. It was also intended to sit on top of the Genius Act, the stablecoin law signed last year. So, stablecoins already have their statute and market structure was the missing half. And the house had done its part a long time ago, passing the bill 294 to 134 in July 2025 with 78 Democrats voting for it. That is about as bipartisan as crypto has ever been in Washington. So then, how does a bill with that much momentum die [clears throat] in the Senate? Well, because somewhere in the 14 months it spent stuck there, it became a partisan issue. Every month of delay attached another argument to it, and by September, none of those arguments were about crypto market structure. No, they were about one family's crypto portfolio. President Trump reported more than 1.4 billion dollars in crypto-related income for 2025, spread across World Liberty Financial, the USD 1 stablecoin, and the Trump meme coin launched days before his second inauguration. World Liberty is run with involvement from Don Jr. and Eric Trump, and it secured conditional approval from the OCC for a national trust bank charter. The widely held view of that was that Trump had become the first president to approve, operate, and regulate a bank connected to his own family. And that's the backdrop every Democrat was voting against. The sponsors knew this, and over last weekend, Senators Lummis, Boozman, and Scott released a 635-page substitute text with more than 100 Democrat requested changes, including a last-minute ethics package. That package barred the president, vice president, members of Congress, judges, and their spouses from issuing new digital assets while in office, forced divestment or blind trusts above a $15,000 interest, and even gave state attorneys general standing to sue. The White House had resisted that one for months. But the Democrats read that and said, "Nope." And their objections were quite specific. The ban only applied going forward, so it touched nothing already earned. Also, it covered issuing tokens, not stablecoin reserve interest or equity sales, which is where most of the money actually was. Enforcement depended on a Justice Department headed by Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense lawyer. And per the more detailed accounts, the whole thing was written to expire in January 2029 anyway. Senator Elizabeth Warren called it, quote, "a weak fig leaf that will do nothing to stop him from making his next $1.4 billion in crypto profits." Senator Lummis said the text was as good as it's going to get, and well, that was that. In the 2024 cycle, the crypto industry's main political spending network, Fairshake, raised over $260 million and spent $140 million across more than 70 congressional races, including around $40 million targeting a single Ohio senator. Coinbase put in $86 million cumulatively, Ripple $45 million. So, going into 2026, Fairshake carried a war chest of about $193 million, and by midyear filings had raised nearly $137 million more for the cycle. Public Citizen's tracking had crypto, AI, and online betting accounting for over $294 million of corporate election spending in the first 15 months of the cycle, with crypto the largest sector of the whole lot. And Fairshake backed candidates won 50 [laughter] of 54 contested primaries. So, the industry did everything it possibly could to push its interests. But apparently, it couldn't buy the remaining votes it needed. And that's because the obstacle was a live battle over conflict of interest involving a sitting president. And there's no campaign contribution that resolves that. Which brings us to the unfortunate reality that this probably spells the end of the Clarity Act, at least in its current form. The Senate never passed its own version of the bill, so there's nothing for lawmakers to merge with the version that already passed the House. And time is basically gone. The House has already left Washington to campaign, while the Senate is about to head into its own break before the midterms. Now, as you can see, crypto regulation can change direction sharply in just a matter of days, which makes these stories very easy to lose track of if you're not watching them closely. So, to make sure you don't miss the major developments that impact your portfolio, come and join us over on the Coin Bureau Telegram channel.
